“So, what brings you in today?” I asked Ben, a 40-year-old man who was sitting across from me.

“Well,” he answered. “I have a few different symptoms. The biggest one is that I am always tired, but I’ve also been gaining weight, and my knees hurt some in the mornings.”

I mentally began to go through what doctors call a differential diagnosis – things that can cause the cluster of symptoms that a patient has. I usually let the patient explain what symptoms he is experiencing and then ask questions to try to hone in on the specific diagnosis.

Ben went on for a little while longer. Then, he proceeded to pull out a piece of paper. “So, Doctor,” he told me. “I’ve done some research into my diagnosis, and I think these are tests that I need to have done to work things up.”

I looked at the list. It was pretty long and included some things I probably would have ordered anyway, like a blood count and thyroid level, but also some very odd things like a Vitamin B1 level and a DHEA level. He also wanted a CT Scan of his head, chest, and abdomen.

“This is a lot of testing,” I said. “I’m not sure we need to do all of it. Can we talk a little bit more about your symptoms and then try to hone in on what testing would be best to sort it out?”

Ben was not impressed. “I have done my research!” He told me firmly. “These days, with the internet, you can find out things that your doctor wouldn’t tell you about – maybe things he doesn’t even know to test for. The problem is that I need YOU to order these things for me so my insurance will cover them. Otherwise, I wouldn’t even be here.”

With that, we’ll leave Ben and his uncomfortable doctor behind. There have always been patients who brought in articles from magazines telling the reader, “Six things your doctor won’t tell you about your health” and listing testing that should be done. It does seem to have gotten worse.

A lot of patients know more than their doctors. They can search for their symptoms on the web and find out all sorts of things that could cause those symptoms.

Beyond that, artificial intelligence is smart. Chat GPT, an artificial intelligence platform, was able to pass the three parts of the US Medical Licensure Exam.1 It didn’t do terribly well— it only got just above a passing grade, but I suppose that’s good enough that it could open an office across the street from mine and start seeing patients.

In some ways letting patients have access to this level of information is a good thing. Doctors aren’t some sort of high priests who are given special rights to access the Holiest of Holies of medical information. More than that, doctors are anything but perfect, and you have only to read online reviews to see that they don’t listen well, botch procedures, and struggle with difficult diagnoses.

It can be challenging, though, when patients believe that they know more than their doctor. I have always said that if you know more than your doctor, either you need a healthy dose of humility or a new doctor— or maybe both.

Get Wisdom!

Proverbs 4:5-9 says, “Get wisdom, get understanding: forget it not; neither decline from the words of my mouth. Forsake her not, and she shall preserve thee: love her, and she shall keep thee. Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding. Exalt her, and she shall promote thee: she shall bring thee to honour, when thou dost embrace her. She shall give to thine head an ornament of grace: a crown of glory shall she deliver to thee.”

Proverbs 18:15 speaks of getting knowledge, but it indicates that before we seek knowledge, we should make certain that we have wisdom and understanding.

The author of the book of Proverbs was Solomon. We know that early in his reign he had a dream in which God appeared to him and offered him whatever he desired. In his humility, Solomon asked for an understanding heart, so that he would be able to wisely lead such a great people (I Kings 3:9,10).

When we look at knowledge, it is simply a group of facts— blocks of information that need to be assembled into some sort of coherent pattern. Wisdom and understanding are the tools with which we make sense of the knowledge that we have acquired.

Wisdom lets us judge the accuracy of the sources of “knowledge” as well. It helps us to ask the question, “Is this person trying to sell me something? Do they actually have any scientific studies that indicate that what they say is true?”

These are two questions that I ask when I look at a website. Are there links to products that are being sold to me, and is the advertising clearly separated from the articles? More than that, are there links to studies that support what is being claimed? If there are, how big were those studies? If a study has only 12 people in it, it is not large enough to give accurate information.

Robert Harris made an acronym CARS, that helps sort out whether information on a website is valid. Credibility, past Accuracy, Reasonableness, and Supporting information are all important to look at to see if we should value the information on a website.2

Unfortunately, many people who claim to have the answers to living long and healthy lives are actually trying to sell books, supplements, and a variety of other products. One prominent doctor who promotes better health through the use of supplements (that he sells) has managed to accrue enough money through the process that he stated in a 2017 affidavit that he was worth in excess of 100 million dollars. This doesn’t mean that he has nothing to offer, but it does say that he has some bias towards recommending things he is selling.

The American Medical Association has guidelines for doctors to sell products out of their offices ethically. Those guidelines say that the products should serve a particular urgent need (say, crutches at an Orthopedic office), have scientific validity for their use, and that doctors should offer information about other ways that patients can get the same products elsewhere.3 More than that, doctors should reveal to their patients any financial interest that they have in the product that is being offered to the patient.

Confirmation Bias

Most of us read in order to confirm the things we already believe. I see this when people read the Bible— somehow, people can read the Bible and completely ignore Scriptures that contradict their behaviors in terms of political involvement or modesty of dress but believe that they are following all things of the Scripture.

In the same way, each one of us can find stories and information that reinforce our beliefs about doctors and medicine. If we believe that doctors are simply after money and are unethical and prescribe medicines that are toxic to patients, we can find articles that confirm that. On the other hand, if we look for stories that tear down alternative medicine theories, we can find those articles too.

The important thing is that we approach the question looking for real answers and understanding that science doesn’t know everything.

As an example, we do not have good treatments for people who have Long COVID symptoms. That doesn’t mean that many people who suffered through COVID months later aren’t suffering from things like mental fog and fatigue, but it does mean that there is not a single medication that has done better than sugar pills in studies to get rid of those symptoms.

In the absence of scientifically proven treatment plans, many clinics have developed their own treatment courses, using a mixture of supplements and even hyperbaric oxygen treatments. Are these helpful? I don’t know, but I do know that those marketing them will confidently claim that they have an extremely high success rate in curing people if they are simply willing to follow (and pay for) the treatment plan.

More than that, when people are researching their symptoms, they tend to choose what diagnoses they think are likely based on their underlying personality types. Some people are prone to catastrophize— that is, they immediately believe the worst possible outcome of any given scenario they are presented with. These people will type in their symptoms and will come to the conclusion that they have cancer with only days or weeks to live. As God told Hezekiah, it is time for them to set their house in order.

On the other hand, there are plenty of people who have optimistic personalities. They type in their symptom list and come to the conclusion that they have a mild viral illness and will feel better in a few days.

The whole point of having a medical provider review things is that the practitioner can (hopefully) sort out the likely things from the unlikely ones. They don’t deal with the emotional overlay that patients do, so they can objectively decide how many tests to order and what type of tests to order in order to come up with a diagnosis.

Doctors Can Identify Dangerous Situations

I remember seeing a patient years ago who came in to see me with what she thought was a sinus infection. She was in her 20s and said that she had a pounding sensation in her head and a lot of pressure.

She didn’t really have any drainage or fever and none of the typical symptoms of a sinus infection, but sinusitis seemed like the most likely diagnosis that she could come up with.

I took one look at her and didn’t like what I saw. For one thing, she was extremely pale. For another, her pulse rate was quite fast – 130 beats a minute at rest. When I examined her, I found nothing that indicated that she had a sinus infection.

“Jenny,” I told her. “I need you to go to the hospital and get a stat blood count. I’m afraid you are really anemic— although I don’t know why. Wait at the lab and I will talk to you once I get the results back.”

It was perhaps 20 minutes later that I got an urgent call from the hospital laboratory. “Dr. Waldron,” the voice on the other end said. “We have a critical lab result for you…”

Jenny’s hemoglobin was 4.6 (normal is between 12 and 16), and she ended up getting a transfusion. What she didn’t get was treatment for a sinus infection.

Chest pain is a classic symptom that can point to an underlying heart condition. At the same time, it could simply indicate esophageal reflux (acid in the esophagus) or inflammation in a rib or muscle. I probably see a couple of patients every day who have this symptom.

The majority of them need a simple treatment, but a few of them need to be sent urgently to the hospital for a complete heart evaluation. I don’t know how an online search engine will know which direction to indicate for a person to seek after reviewing their symptoms.

At best, an online resource will refer a user to seek emergency services or their local doctor.

Not All Doctors Are Equal

Roughly 50 percent of doctors finished in the bottom half of their Medical School class. Just because someone didn’t have top marks in Medical School doesn’t mean that they don’t have adequate knowledge to treat an ailment. Perhaps the most important knowledge that a doctor needs is to know when he doesn’t know.

It is still challenging for patients to know whether they are dealing with someone who will help them. When you meet a doctor, you tend to judge them based on their “bedside manner.” Most of us look for someone who exudes confidence and seems to know what they are doing.

Confidence does not equal competence, and there are many doctors (and people in other fields) who have high levels of confidence in themselves but are not really competent to take care of the situation at hand.

Here is where doing some research can help. First, your doctor has online reviews, and those reviews will indicate something about the level of care they provide for patients. Second, if what your healthcare provider tells you seems really odd, it is easy to do a little research on the condition that you are supposedly dealing with and see if the symptoms line up and if the treatment seems reasonable.

It is important to realize that humans are not like vehicles. What I mean by that is that there is no scan tool that healthcare providers can hook up and generate all of the error codes and then fix the things that generate those codes.

Even if healthcare providers are certain of the diagnosis, some patients do not respond to the first or even the second treatment that is available. That doesn’t mean that the diagnosis or the treatment was wrong, but that people are not clones of each other and some respond better to one type of treatment than another.

Maybe someday we will have some type of genetic testing that tells us right off what the perfect medication or treatment plan is for a given illness, but that day seems a long way off.

A final thing to mention is that good doctors will not feel threatened by their patients asking questions or doing research. There are times when a patient will ask me about a new treatment that I am not familiar with, and I need to do my own research.

Those scenarios are not upsetting for me but rather a learning opportunity. “I’m not familiar with that,” I will tell my patient. “Let me do a little research and talk to some specialists that I trust, and I will call you later this week and let you know what I find out.”

Sometimes I investigate and find that the treatment is expensive and seems to provide mixed or little benefit, but sometimes it is an improvement over the past ways of doing things. Doctors need to learn and adjust their style of practicing medicine as we learn new things about diseases and how the human body responds to them.

Humility is Needed

The longer I practice medicine, the less I feel that I know. It isn’t that I have developed dementia, but rather that I realize that there are numerous diseases that we don’t have good treatments for. The human body is amazingly complex. There are 36 trillion cells in the human body, and normally, they all work together perfectly; the problem is figuring out what to do when they don’t.

The Dunning-Kruger Effect is something that affects many fields in which people with limited knowledge and skill significantly overestimate their abilities in that field. Studies have shown that 65 percent of Americans believe that they have above-average IQs.4 Statistically, this isn’t possible. Fifty percent of any group of people will have above-average IQs, and the other 50 percent will be below-average. That’s how the IQ scale is set up.

While this effect is present for doctors, it is also present for patients. “Doing your research” is not the same thing as spending four years in Medical School, another three years in a residency training program, and continuing to stay abreast of developments in medicine through a variety of educational courses. We all would do well to listen better and realize our limitations.

The fact that your mother’s cousin took milkweed extract and felt much better from similar symptoms to yours is interesting. Whether the milkweed extract helped them get over their illness, whether there was a placebo effect, or they were just going to get better anyway, regardless of what they took, is up for debate.

True Wisdom

I have mentioned wisdom already, and I would finish with that. True wisdom is realizing that healing comes from God. Psalms 103:3 says of God, “Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases.”

Healing doesn’t come from antibiotics or chemotherapy. It doesn’t come from taking the right supplements or even eating a healthy diet. Healing comes because God touches us, right down to the tiniest parts of our cells and immune system, and makes things whole again.

I do believe that sometimes He works through medicine, but other times He works through the effective, fervent prayer of righteous men and women. (James 5:16)

With all of our knowledge, it is easy for us to get puffed up with pride and believe that we need no one else. We live in a world that is teeming with knowledge and a world in which wisdom has taken a back seat.

We must choose the source of our information carefully and realize that we don’t know everything. Maybe the reason why the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom is because it is the first step to us laying aside our pride and realizing that we are a tiny part of Creation. Only then, can we humbly listen and learn and receive healing.

Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding. Exalt her, and she shall promote thee: she shall bring thee to honour, when thou dost embrace her. She shall give to thine head an ornament of grace: a crown of glory shall she deliver to thee.”

Proverbs 18:15 speaks of getting knowledge, but it indicates that before we seek knowledge, we should make certain that we have wisdom and understanding.

The author of the book of Proverbs was Solomon. We know that early in his reign he had a dream in which God appeared to him and offered him whatever he desired. In his humility, Solomon asked for an understanding heart, so that he would be able to wisely lead such a great people (I Kings 3:9,10).

When we look at knowledge, it is simply a group of facts— blocks of information that need to be assembled into some sort of coherent pattern. Wisdom and understanding are the tools with which we make sense of the knowledge that we have acquired.

Wisdom lets us judge the accuracy of the sources of “knowledge” as well. It helps us to ask the question, “Is this person trying to sell me something? Do they actually have any scientific studies that indicate that what they say is true?”

These are two questions that I ask when I look at a website. Are there links to products that are being sold to me, and is the advertising clearly separated from the articles? More than that, are there links to studies that support what is being claimed? If there are, how big were those studies? If a study has only 12 people in it, it is not large enough to give accurate information.

Robert Harris made an acronym CARS, that helps sort out whether information on a website is valid. Credibility, past Accuracy, Reasonableness, and Supporting information are all important to look at to see if we should value the information on a website.2

Unfortunately, many people who claim to have the answers to living long and healthy lives are actually trying to sell books, supplements, and a variety of other products. One prominent doctor who promotes better health through the use of supplements (that he sells) has managed to accrue enough money through the process that he stated in a 2017 affidavit that he was worth in excess of 100 million dollars. This doesn’t mean that he has nothing to offer, but it does say that he has some bias towards recommending things he is selling.

The American Medical Association has guidelines for doctors to sell products out of their offices ethically. Those guidelines say that the products should serve a particular urgent need (say, crutches at an Orthopedic office), have scientific validity for their use, and that doctors should offer information about other ways that patients can get the same products elsewhere.3 More than that, doctors should reveal to their patients any financial interest that they have in the product that is being offered to the patient.

Confirmation Bias

Most of us read in order to confirm the things we already believe. I see this when people read the Bible— somehow, people can read the Bible and completely ignore Scriptures that contradict their behaviors in terms of political involvement or modesty of dress but believe that they are following all things of the Scripture.

In the same way, each one of us can find stories and information that reinforce our beliefs about doctors and medicine. If we believe that doctors are simply after money and are unethical and prescribe medicines that are toxic to patients, we can find articles that confirm that. On the other hand, if we look for stories that tear down alternative medicine theories, we can find those articles too.

The important thing is that we approach the question looking for real answers and understanding that science doesn’t know everything.

As an example, we do not have good treatments for people who have Long COVID symptoms. That doesn’t mean that many people who suffered through COVID months later aren’t suffering from things like mental fog and fatigue, but it does mean that there is not a single medication that has done better than sugar pills in studies to get rid of those symptoms.

In the absence of scientifically proven treatment plans, many clinics have developed their own treatment courses, using a mixture of supplements and even hyperbaric oxygen treatments. Are these helpful? I don’t know, but I do know that those marketing them will confidently claim that they have an extremely high success rate in curing people if they are simply willing to follow (and pay for) the treatment plan.

More than that, when people are researching their symptoms, they tend to choose what diagnoses they think are likely based on their underlying personality types. Some people are prone to catastrophize— that is, they immediately believe the worst possible outcome of any given scenario they are presented with. These people will type in their symptoms and will come to the conclusion that they have cancer with only days or weeks to live. As God told Hezekiah, it is time for them to set their house in order.

On the other hand, there are plenty of people who have optimistic personalities. They type in their symptom list and come to the conclusion that they have a mild viral illness and will feel better in a few days.

The whole point of having a medical provider review things is that the practitioner can (hopefully) sort out the likely things from the unlikely ones. They don’t deal with the emotional overlay that patients do, so they can objectively decide how many tests to order and what type of tests to order in order to come up with a diagnosis.

Doctors Can Identify Dangerous Situations

I remember seeing a patient years ago who came in to see me with what she thought was a sinus infection. She was in her 20s and said that she had a pounding sensation in her head and a lot of pressure.

She didn’t really have any drainage or fever and none of the typical symptoms of a sinus infection, but sinusitis seemed like the most likely diagnosis that she could come up with.

I took one look at her and didn’t like what I saw. For one thing, she was extremely pale. For another, her pulse rate was quite fast – 130 beats a minute at rest. When I examined her, I found nothing that indicated that she had a sinus infection.

“Jenny,” I told her. “I need you to go to the hospital and get a stat blood count. I’m afraid you are really anemic— although I don’t know why. Wait at the lab and I will talk to you once I get the results back.”

It was perhaps 20 minutes later that I got an urgent call from the hospital laboratory. “Dr. Waldron,” the voice on the other end said. “We have a critical lab result for you…”

Jenny’s hemoglobin was 4.6 (normal is between 12 and 16), and she ended up getting a transfusion. What she didn’t get was treatment for a sinus infection.

Chest pain is a classic symptom that can point to an underlying heart condition. At the same time, it could simply indicate esophageal reflux (acid in the esophagus) or inflammation in a rib or muscle. I probably see a couple of patients every day who have this symptom.

The majority of them need a simple treatment, but a few of them need to be sent urgently to the hospital for a complete heart evaluation. I don’t know how an online search engine will know which direction to indicate for a person to seek after reviewing their symptoms.

At best, an online resource will refer a user to seek emergency services or their local doctor.

Not All Doctors Are Equal

Roughly 50 percent of doctors finished in the bottom half of their Medical School class. Just because someone didn’t have top marks in Medical School doesn’t mean that they don’t have adequate knowledge to treat an ailment. Perhaps the most important knowledge that a doctor needs is to know when he doesn’t know.

It is still challenging for patients to know whether they are dealing with someone who will help them. When you meet a doctor, you tend to judge them based on their “bedside manner.” Most of us look for someone who exudes confidence and seems to know what they are doing.

Confidence does not equal competence, and there are many doctors (and people in other fields) who have high levels of confidence in themselves but are not really competent to take care of the situation at hand.

Here is where doing some research can help. First, your doctor has online reviews, and those reviews will indicate something about the level of care they provide for patients. Second, if what your healthcare provider tells you seems really odd, it is easy to do a little research on the condition that you are supposedly dealing with and see if the symptoms line up and if the treatment seems reasonable.

It is important to realize that humans are not like vehicles. What I mean by that is that there is no scan tool that healthcare providers can hook up and generate all of the error codes and then fix the things that generate those codes.

Even if healthcare providers are certain of the diagnosis, some patients do not respond to the first or even the second treatment that is available. That doesn’t mean that the diagnosis or the treatment was wrong, but that people are not clones of each other and some respond better to one type of treatment than another.

Maybe someday we will have some type of genetic testing that tells us right off what the perfect medication or treatment plan is for a given illness, but that day seems a long way off.

A final thing to mention is that good doctors will not feel threatened by their patients asking questions or doing research. There are times when a patient will ask me about a new treatment that I am not familiar with, and I need to do my own research.

Those scenarios are not upsetting for me but rather a learning opportunity. “I’m not familiar with that,” I will tell my patient. “Let me do a little research and talk to some specialists that I trust, and I will call you later this week and let you know what I find out.”

Sometimes I investigate and find that the treatment is expensive and seems to provide mixed or little benefit, but sometimes it is an improvement over the past ways of doing things. Doctors need to learn and adjust their style of practicing medicine as we learn new things about diseases and how the human body responds to them.

Humility is Needed

The longer I practice medicine, the less I feel that I know. It isn’t that I have developed dementia, but rather that I realize that there are numerous diseases that we don’t have good treatments for. The human body is amazingly complex. There are 36 trillion cells in the human body, and normally, they all work together perfectly; the problem is figuring out what to do when they don’t.

The Dunning-Kruger Effect is something that affects many fields in which people with limited knowledge and skill significantly overestimate their abilities in that field. Studies have shown that 65 percent of Americans believe that they have above-average IQs.4 Statistically, this isn’t possible. Fifty percent of any group of people will have above-average IQs, and the other 50 percent will be below-average. That’s how the IQ scale is set up.

While this effect is present for doctors, it is also present for patients. “Doing your research” is not the same thing as spending four years in Medical School, another three years in a residency training program, and continuing to stay abreast of developments in medicine through a variety of educational courses. We all would do well to listen better and realize our limitations.

The fact that your mother’s cousin took milkweed extract and felt much better from similar symptoms to yours is interesting. Whether the milkweed extract helped them get over their illness, whether there was a placebo effect, or they were just going to get better anyway, regardless of what they took, is up for debate.

True Wisdom

I have mentioned wisdom already, and I would finish with that. True wisdom is realizing that healing comes from God. Psalms 103:3 says of God, “Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases.”

Healing doesn’t come from antibiotics or chemotherapy. It doesn’t come from taking the right supplements or even eating a healthy diet. Healing comes because God touches us, right down to the tiniest parts of our cells and immune system, and makes things whole again.

I do believe that sometimes He works through medicine, but other times He works through the effective, fervent prayer of righteous men and women. (James 5:16)

With all of our knowledge, it is easy for us to get puffed up with pride and believe that we need no one else. We live in a world that is teeming with knowledge and a world in which wisdom has taken a back seat.

We must choose the source of our information carefully and realize that we don’t know everything. Maybe the reason why the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom is because it is the first step to us laying aside our pride and realizing that we are a tiny part of Creation. Only then, can we humbly listen and learn and receive healing.

“Então, o que o traz aqui hoje?” perguntei a Ben, um homem de 40 anos que estava sentado à minha frente.

“Bem,” ele respondeu. “Tenho alguns sintomas diferentes. O maior é que estou sempre cansado, mas também tenho ganhado peso e meus joelhos doem um pouco de manhã.”

Comecei mentalmente a passar pelo que os médicos chamam de diagnóstico diferencial — coisas que podem causar o conjunto de sintomas que um paciente apresenta. Geralmente deixo o paciente explicar quais sintomas ele está experimentando e então faço perguntas para tentar acertar o diagnóstico específico.

Ben continuou por mais um pouco. Depois, ele tirou um pedaço de papel. “Então, doutor,” ele me disse. “Fiz uma pesquisa sobre meu diagnóstico e acho que estes são os exames que preciso fazer para investigar.”

Olhei a lista. Era bem longa e incluía algumas coisas que eu provavelmente teria solicitado de qualquer forma, como um hemograma e níveis de tireoide, mas também algumas coisas muito estranhas, como um nível de vitamina B1 e um nível de DHEA. Ele também queria uma tomografia computadorizada da cabeça, tórax e abdome.

“São muitos exames,” disse. “Não tenho certeza de que precisamos fazer todos eles. Podemos conversar um pouco mais sobre seus sintomas e então tentar definir quais exames seriam melhores para esclarecer isso?”

Ben não ficou impressionado. “Eu pesquisei!” disse-me firmemente. “Hoje em dia, com a internet, você pode descobrir coisas que seu médico não lhe diria — talvez coisas que ele nem saiba testar. O problema é que eu preciso que VOCÊ peça essas coisas para mim para que meu seguro as cubra. Caso contrário, eu nem estaria aqui.”

Com isso, deixaremos Ben e seu médico desconfortável para trás. Sempre houve pacientes que traziam artigos de revistas dizendo ao leitor, “Seis coisas que seu médico não lhe dirá sobre sua saúde” e listando exames que deveriam ser feitos. Parece que isso piorou.

Muitos pacientes sabem mais do que seus médicos. Podem pesquisar seus sintomas na web e descobrir todo tipo de coisa que poderia causar esses sintomas.

Além disso, a inteligência artificial é inteligente. O ChatGPT, uma plataforma de inteligência artificial, foi capaz de passar nas três partes do Exame de Licença Médica dos EUA.1 Não foi um desempenho excelente — obteve apenas um pouco acima da nota de aprovação, mas suponho que isso seja suficiente para que pudesse abrir um consultório do outro lado da rua e começar a atender pacientes.

Em certo sentido, permitir que os pacientes tenham acesso a esse nível de informação é uma coisa boa. Os médicos não são uma espécie de sacerdotes que têm direitos especiais de acessar o Santo dos Santos da informação médica. Além disso, os médicos estão longe de ser perfeitos, e basta ler avaliações online para ver que eles não escutam bem, cometem erros em procedimentos e têm dificuldades com diagnósticos complicados.

Porém, pode ser desafiador quando os pacientes acreditam que sabem mais do que seu médico. Sempre disse que se você sabe mais do que seu médico, ou precisa de uma boa dose de humildade ou de um novo médico — ou talvez ambos.

Adquira sabedoria!

Provérbios 4:5-9 diz: “Adquire a sabedoria, adquire a inteligência; não te esqueças nem te apartes das palavras da minha boca. Não a abandones, e ela te guardará; ama-a, e ela cuidará de ti. A sabedoria é a principal coisa; adquire, pois, a sabedoria; e com tudo o que possuíres adquire o entendimento. Exalta-a, e ela te exaltará; e, quando a abraçares, ela te honrará. Ela dará à tua cabeça uma graciosidade; uma coroa de glória te entregará.”

Provérbios 18:15 fala de adquirir conhecimento, mas indica que, antes de buscarmos conhecimento, devemos ter certeza de que possuímos sabedoria e entendimento.

O autor do livro de Provérbios foi Salomão. Sabemos que no início de seu reinado ele teve um sonho em que Deus lhe apareceu e lhe ofereceu o que quer que desejasse. Em sua humildade, Salomão pediu um coração entendido, para que pudesse conduzir sabiamente um povo tão grande (I Reis 3:9,10).

Quando olhamos para o conhecimento, ele é simplesmente um conjunto de fatos — blocos de informação que precisam ser montados em algum tipo de padrão coerente. Sabedoria e entendimento são as ferramentas com as quais damos sentido ao conhecimento que adquirimos.

A sabedoria também nos permite julgar a precisão das fontes de “conhecimento”. Ela nos ajuda a fazer a pergunta: “Esta pessoa está tentando me vender algo? Ela tem realmente algum estudo científico que indique que o que diz é verdadeiro?”

Essas são duas perguntas que faço quando analiso um site. Existem links para produtos que estão sendo vendidos para mim, e a publicidade está claramente separada dos artigos? Além disso, há links para estudos que apoiem o que está sendo alegado? Se houver, qual o tamanho desses estudos? Se um estudo tem apenas 12 pessoas, não é grande o suficiente para fornecer informação precisa.

Robert Harris criou o acrônimo CARS, que ajuda a separar se a informação em um site é válida. Credibilidade, Precisão passada, Razoabilidade e Informações de suporte são tudo importante de considerar para ver se devemos valorizar a informação em um site.2

Infelizmente, muitas pessoas que afirmam ter as respostas para viver vidas longas e saudáveis estão, na verdade, tentando vender livros, suplementos e uma variedade de outros produtos. Um médico proeminente que promove melhor saúde por meio do uso de suplementos (que ele vende) conseguiu acumular tanto dinheiro através desse processo que afirmou em uma declaração juramentada de 2017 que valia mais de 100 milhões de dólares. Isso não significa que ele não tenha nada a oferecer, mas indica que tem um viés a favorecer as coisas que está vendendo.

A American Medical Association tem diretrizes para médicos venderem produtos em seus consultórios de maneira ética. Essas diretrizes dizem que os produtos devem atender a uma necessidade particular urgente (por exemplo, muletas em um consultório de ortopedia), ter validade científica para seu uso, e que os médicos devem oferecer informações sobre outras formas de os pacientes adquirirem os mesmos produtos em outro lugar.3 Além disso, os médicos devem revelar a seus pacientes qualquer interesse financeiro que tenham no produto que está sendo oferecido.

Viés de confirmação

A maioria de nós lê para confirmar as coisas que já acreditamos. Vejo isso quando as pessoas leem a Bíblia — de alguma forma, as pessoas podem ler as Escrituras e ignorar completamente passagens que contradizem seus comportamentos em termos de envolvimento político ou modéstia no vestir-se, mas acreditam que estão seguindo tudo o que a Escritura manda.

Da mesma forma, cada um de nós pode encontrar histórias e informações que reforcem nossas crenças sobre médicos e medicina. Se acreditamos que os médicos estão apenas atrás de dinheiro, são antiéticos e prescrevem medicamentos tóxicos aos pacientes, podemos encontrar artigos que confirmem isso. Por outro lado, se procurarmos histórias que derrubem teorias de medicina alternativa, também as encontraremos.

O importante é que abordemos a questão buscando respostas reais e entendendo que a ciência não sabe tudo.

Por exemplo, não temos bons tratamentos para pessoas que apresentam sintomas de COVID longa. Isso não significa que muitas pessoas que sofreram com COVID meses depois não estejam sofrendo de coisas como névoa mental e fadiga, mas significa que não há um único medicamento que tenha se saído melhor do que comprimidos de açúcar (placebo) em estudos para eliminar esses sintomas.

Na ausência de planos de tratamento cientificamente comprovados, muitas clínicas desenvolveram seus próprios cursos de tratamento, usando uma mistura de suplementos e até tratamentos com oxigênio hiperbárico. Isso é útil? Não sei, mas sei que quem os comercializa afirmará com confiança ter uma taxa de sucesso extremamente alta em curar as pessoas, desde que estejam dispostas a seguir (e pagar por) o plano de tratamento.

Além disso, quando as pessoas pesquisam seus sintomas, tendem a escolher os diagnósticos que consideram prováveis com base em seus traços de personalidade subjacentes. Algumas pessoas são propensas a catastrofizar — isto é, acreditam imediatamente no pior resultado possível de qualquer cenário apresentado. Essas pessoas irão digitar seus sintomas e chegar à conclusão de que têm câncer e apenas dias ou semanas de vida. Como Deus disse a Ezequias, é hora de pôr sua casa em ordem.

Por outro lado, há muitas pessoas com personalidades otimistas. Digitam sua lista de sintomas e concluem que têm uma doença viral leve e vão melhorar em alguns dias.

O objetivo de ter um profissional médico revisando as coisas é que o praticante possa (esperançosamente) separar o que é provável do que é improvável. Eles não lidam com a sobreposição emocional que os pacientes têm, de modo que podem decidir objetivamente quantos exames pedir e que tipo de exames solicitar para chegar a um diagnóstico.

Os médicos podem identificar situações perigosas

Lembro-me de ver uma paciente anos atrás que veio me ver achando que tinha uma sinusite. Estava na casa dos 20 anos e disse que sentia uma pulsação forte na cabeça e muita pressão.

Ela não tinha realmente secreção ou febre e nenhum dos sintomas típicos de uma sinusite, mas sinusite parecia o diagnóstico mais provável que ela conseguiu imaginar.

Olhei para ela e não gostei do que vi. Por um lado, estava extremamente pálida. Por outro, sua frequência cardíaca estava bastante alta — 130 batimentos por minuto em repouso. Ao examiná-la, não encontrei nada que indicasse que tinha uma sinusite.

“Jenny,” disse-lhe. “Preciso que você vá ao hospital e faça um hemograma urgente. Receio que você esteja realmente anêmica — embora eu não saiba por quê. Espere no laboratório que eu conversarei com você assim que receber os resultados.”

Foi talvez 20 minutos depois que recebi uma ligação urgente do laboratório do hospital. “Dra. Waldron,” disse a voz do outro lado. “Temos um resultado laboratorial crítico para você…”

O hemoglobina de Jenny era 4,6 (o normal fica entre 12 e 16), e ela acabou recebendo uma transfusão. O que ela não recebeu foi tratamento para uma sinusite.

A dor no peito é um sintoma clássico que pode apontar para uma condição cardíaca subjacente. Ao mesmo tempo, pode simplesmente indicar refluxo esofágico (ácido no esôfago) ou inflamação em uma costela ou músculo. Provavelmente atendo um par de pacientes por dia com esse sintoma.

A maioria precisa de um tratamento simples, mas alguns precisam ser enviados com urgência ao hospital para uma avaliação cardíaca completa. Não sei como um mecanismo de busca online saberia que direção indicar a uma pessoa ao revisar seus sintomas.

No melhor dos casos, um recurso online encaminhará o usuário a procurar serviços de emergência ou seu médico local.

Nem todos os médicos são iguais

Cerca de 50% dos médicos terminaram na metade inferior de sua turma na escola de medicina. Só porque alguém não teve as melhores notas na faculdade de medicina não significa que não tenha conhecimento adequado para tratar uma enfermidade. Talvez o conhecimento mais importante que um médico precisa seja saber quando ele não sabe.

Ainda é desafiador para os pacientes saberem se estão lidando com alguém que os ajudará. Ao conhecer um médico, tendemos a julgá-lo com base em sua “maneira de atender”. A maioria de nós procura alguém que exale confiança e pareça saber o que está fazendo.

Confiança não é igual a competência, e há muitos médicos (e pessoas em outros campos) que têm altos níveis de confiança em si mesmos, mas não são realmente competentes para lidar com a situação em questão.

Aqui é onde fazer alguma pesquisa pode ajudar. Primeiro, seu médico tem avaliações online, e essas avaliações indicarão algo sobre o nível de cuidado que ele presta aos pacientes. Segundo, se o que seu profissional de saúde lhe diz parece realmente estranho, é fácil fazer uma pequena pesquisa sobre a condição com a qual você supostamente está lidando e ver se os sintomas batem e se o tratamento parece razoável.

É importante perceber que os humanos não são como veículos. O que quero dizer com isso é que não existe uma ferramenta de escaneamento que os profissionais de saúde possam conectar e gerar todos os códigos de erro e então consertar as coisas que geram esses códigos.

Mesmo quando os profissionais de saúde estão certos do diagnóstico, alguns pacientes não respondem ao primeiro ou mesmo ao segundo tratamento disponível. Isso não significa que o diagnóstico ou o tratamento estava errado, mas que as pessoas não são clones umas das outras e algumas respondem melhor a um tipo de tratamento do que a outro.

Talvez algum dia teremos algum tipo de teste genético que nos diga imediatamente qual o medicamento ou plano de tratamento perfeito para uma determinada doença, mas esse dia parece distante.

Uma última observação é que bons médicos não se sentirão ameaçados por pacientes que fazem perguntas ou pesquisam. Há ocasiões em que um paciente me pergunta sobre um novo tratamento com o qual não estou familiarizado, e preciso fazer minha própria pesquisa.

Esses cenários não me perturbam, mas são uma oportunidade de aprendizado. “Não estou familiarizado com isso,” direi ao meu paciente. “Deixe-me pesquisar um pouco e falar com alguns especialistas em quem confio, e eu ligarei para você no final da semana e direi o que descobri.”

Às vezes investigo e descubro que o tratamento é caro e parece oferecer benefícios mistos ou pequenos, mas às vezes é uma melhoria em relação às formas antigas de tratamento. Os médicos precisam aprender e ajustar seu estilo de prática médica à medida que aprendemos coisas novas sobre doenças e como o corpo humano responde a elas.

Humildade é necessária

Quanto mais tempo pratico medicina, menos sinto que sei. Não é que eu tenha desenvolvido demência, mas sim que percebo que há inúmeras doenças para as quais não temos bons tratamentos. O corpo humano é incrivelmente complexo. Há 36 trilhões de células no corpo humano e, normalmente, todas trabalham juntas perfeitamente; o problema é descobrir o que fazer quando não funcionam.

O Efeito Dunning-Kruger é algo que afeta muitos campos em que pessoas com conhecimento e habilidade limitados superestimam significativamente suas capacidades nessa área. Estudos mostraram que 65% dos americanos acreditam ter QI acima da média.4 Estatisticamente, isso não é possível. Cinquenta por cento de qualquer grupo de pessoas terá QI acima da média, e os outros 50% estarão abaixo da média. É assim que a escala de QI é configurada.

Embora esse efeito esteja presente entre médicos, também está presente entre pacientes. “Fazer sua pesquisa” não é o mesmo que passar quatro anos na faculdade de medicina, outros três anos em um programa de residência e continuar a se manter atualizado sobre desenvolvimentos na medicina por meio de uma variedade de cursos educacionais. Todos nós faríamos bem em ouvir mais e perceber nossas limitações.

O fato de o primo da sua mãe ter tomado extrato de planta-podre e ter se sentido muito melhor de sintomas semelhantes aos seus é interessante. Se o extrato ajudou a pessoa a superar a doença, se houve efeito placebo ou se ela simplesmente iria melhorar de qualquer forma, independentemente do que tomou, isso é discutível.

Verdadeira sabedoria

Já mencionei a sabedoria, e gostaria de concluir com isso. A verdadeira sabedoria é perceber que a cura vem de Deus. Salmos 103:3 diz de Deus: “Que perdoa todas as tuas iniquidades; que sara todas as tuas enfermidades.”

A cura não vem de antibióticos ou quimioterapia. Não vem de tomar os suplementos certos ou mesmo de ter uma dieta saudável. A cura vem porque Deus nos toca, até as menores partes de nossas células e do nosso sistema imunológico, e torna as coisas inteiras novamente.

Acredito que às vezes Ele trabalha por meio da medicina, mas outras vezes trabalha por meio da oração eficaz e fervorosa de homens e mulheres justos. (Tiago 5:16)

Com todo o nosso conhecimento, é fácil ficarmos cheios de orgulho e acreditar que não precisamos de mais ninguém. Vivemos em um mundo repleto de conhecimento e onde a sabedoria ficou em segundo plano.

Devemos escolher cuidadosamente a fonte de nossa informação e perceber que não sabemos tudo. Talvez a razão pela qual “o temor do Senhor é o princípio da sabedoria” seja porque é o primeiro passo para deixarmos de lado nosso orgulho e percebermos que somos uma pequena parte da Criação. Só então podemos humildemente ouvir, aprender e receber cura.

“So, what brings you in today?” I asked Ben, a 40-year-old man who was sitting across from me.

“Well,” he answered. “I have a few different symptoms. The biggest one is that I am always tired, but I’ve also been gaining weight, and my knees hurt some in the mornings.”

I mentally began to go through what doctors call a differential diagnosis – things that can cause the cluster of symptoms that a patient has. I usually let the patient explain what symptoms he is experiencing and then ask questions to try to hone in on the specific diagnosis.

Ben went on for a little while longer. Then, he proceeded to pull out a piece of paper. “So, Doctor,” he told me. “I’ve done some research into my diagnosis, and I think these are tests that I need to have done to work things up.”

I looked at the list. It was pretty long and included some things I probably would have ordered anyway, like a blood count and thyroid level, but also some very odd things like a Vitamin B1 level and a DHEA level. He also wanted a CT Scan of his head, chest, and abdomen.

“This is a lot of testing,” I said. “I’m not sure we need to do all of it. Can we talk a little bit more about your symptoms and then try to hone in on what testing would be best to sort it out?”

Ben was not impressed. “I have done my research!” He told me firmly. “These days, with the internet, you can find out things that your doctor wouldn’t tell you about – maybe things he doesn’t even know to test for. The problem is that I need YOU to order these things for me so my insurance will cover them. Otherwise, I wouldn’t even be here.”

With that, we’ll leave Ben and his uncomfortable doctor behind. There have always been patients who brought in articles from magazines telling the reader, “Six things your doctor won’t tell you about your health” and listing testing that should be done. It does seem to have gotten worse.

A lot of patients know more than their doctors. They can search for their symptoms on the web and find out all sorts of things that could cause those symptoms.

Beyond that, artificial intelligence is smart. Chat GPT, an artificial intelligence platform, was able to pass the three parts of the US Medical Licensure Exam.1 It didn’t do terribly well— it only got just above a passing grade, but I suppose that’s good enough that it could open an office across the street from mine and start seeing patients.

In some ways letting patients have access to this level of information is a good thing. Doctors aren’t some sort of high priests who are given special rights to access the Holiest of Holies of medical information. More than that, doctors are anything but perfect, and you have only to read online reviews to see that they don’t listen well, botch procedures, and struggle with difficult diagnoses.

It can be challenging, though, when patients believe that they know more than their doctor. I have always said that if you know more than your doctor, either you need a healthy dose of humility or a new doctor— or maybe both.

Get Wisdom!

Proverbs 4:5-9 says, “Get wisdom, get understanding: forget it not; neither decline from the words of my mouth. Forsake her not, and she shall preserve thee: love her, and she shall keep thee. Wisdom is the principal thing; therefore get wisdom: and with all thy getting get understanding. Exalt her, and she shall promote thee: she shall bring thee to honour, when thou dost embrace her. She shall give to thine head an ornament of grace: a crown of glory shall she deliver to thee.”

Proverbs 18:15 speaks of getting knowledge, but it indicates that before we seek knowledge, we should make certain that we have wisdom and understanding.

The author of the book of Proverbs was Solomon. We know that early in his reign he had a dream in which God appeared to him and offered him whatever he desired. In his humility, Solomon asked for an understanding heart, so that he would be able to wisely lead such a great people (I Kings 3:9,10).

When we look at knowledge, it is simply a group of facts— blocks of information that need to be assembled into some sort of coherent pattern. Wisdom and understanding are the tools with which we make sense of the knowledge that we have acquired.

Wisdom lets us judge the accuracy of the sources of “knowledge” as well. It helps us to ask the question, “Is this person trying to sell me something? Do they actually have any scientific studies that indicate that what they say is true?”

These are two questions that I ask when I look at a website. Are there links to products that are being sold to me, and is the advertising clearly separated from the articles? More than that, are there links to studies that support what is being claimed? If there are, how big were those studies? If a study has only 12 people in it, it is not large enough to give accurate information.

Robert Harris made an acronym CARS, that helps sort out whether information on a website is valid. Credibility, past Accuracy, Reasonableness, and Supporting information are all important to look at to see if we should value the information on a website.2

Unfortunately, many people who claim to have the answers to living long and healthy lives are actually trying to sell books, supplements, and a variety of other products. One prominent doctor who promotes better health through the use of supplements (that he sells) has managed to accrue enough money through the process that he stated in a 2017 affidavit that he was worth in excess of 100 million dollars. This doesn’t mean that he has nothing to offer, but it does say that he has some bias towards recommending things he is selling.

The American Medical Association has guidelines for doctors to sell products out of their offices ethically. Those guidelines say that the products should serve a particular urgent need (say, crutches at an Orthopedic office), have scientific validity for their use, and that doctors should offer information about other ways that patients can get the same products elsewhere.3 More than that, doctors should reveal to their patients any financial interest that they have in the product that is being offered to the patient.

Confirmation Bias

Most of us read in order to confirm the things we already believe. I see this when people read the Bible— somehow, people can read the Bible and completely ignore Scriptures that contradict their behaviors in terms of political involvement or modesty of dress but believe that they are following all things of the Scripture.

In the same way, each one of us can find stories and information that reinforce our beliefs about doctors and medicine. If we believe that doctors are simply after money and are unethical and prescribe medicines that are toxic to patients, we can find articles that confirm that. On the other hand, if we look for stories that tear down alternative medicine theories, we can find those articles too.

The important thing is that we approach the question looking for real answers and understanding that science doesn’t know everything.

As an example, we do not have good treatments for people who have Long COVID symptoms. That doesn’t mean that many people who suffered through COVID months later aren’t suffering from things like mental fog and fatigue, but it does mean that there is not a single medication that has done better than sugar pills in studies to get rid of those symptoms.

In the absence of scientifically proven treatment plans, many clinics have developed their own treatment courses, using a mixture of supplements and even hyperbaric oxygen treatments. Are these helpful? I don’t know, but I do know that those marketing them will confidently claim that they have an extremely high success rate in curing people if they are simply willing to follow (and pay for) the treatment plan.

More than that, when people are researching their symptoms, they tend to choose what diagnoses they think are likely based on their underlying personality types. Some people are prone to catastrophize— that is, they immediately believe the worst possible outcome of any given scenario they are presented with. These people will type in their symptoms and will come to the conclusion that they have cancer with only days or weeks to live. As God told Hezekiah, it is time for them to set their house in order.

On the other hand, there are plenty of people who have optimistic personalities. They type in their symptom list and come to the conclusion that they have a mild viral illness and will feel better in a few days.

The whole point of having a medical provider review things is that the practitioner can (hopefully) sort out the likely things from the unlikely ones. They don’t deal with the emotional overlay that patients do, so they can objectively decide how many tests to order and what type of tests to order in order to come up with a diagnosis.

Doctors Can Identify Dangerous Situations

I remember seeing a patient years ago who came in to see me with what she thought was a sinus infection. She was in her 20s and said that she had a pounding sensation in her head and a lot of pressure.

She didn’t really have any drainage or fever and none of the typical symptoms of a sinus infection, but sinusitis seemed like the most likely diagnosis that she could come up with.

I took one look at her and didn’t like what I saw. For one thing, she was extremely pale. For another, her pulse rate was quite fast – 130 beats a minute at rest. When I examined her, I found nothing that indicated that she had a sinus infection.

“Jenny,” I told her. “I need you to go to the hospital and get a stat blood count. I’m afraid you are really anemic— although I don’t know why. Wait at the lab and I will talk to you once I get the results back.”

It was perhaps 20 minutes later that I got an urgent call from the hospital laboratory. “Dr. Waldron,” the voice on the other end said. “We have a critical lab result for you…”

Jenny’s hemoglobin was 4.6 (normal is between 12 and 16), and she ended up getting a transfusion. What she didn’t get was treatment for a sinus infection.

Chest pain is a classic symptom that can point to an underlying heart condition. At the same time, it could simply indicate esophageal reflux (acid in the esophagus) or inflammation in a rib or muscle. I probably see a couple of patients every day who have this symptom.

The majority of them need a simple treatment, but a few of them need to be sent urgently to the hospital for a complete heart evaluation. I don’t know how an online search engine will know which direction to indicate for a person to seek after reviewing their symptoms.

At best, an online resource will refer a user to seek emergency services or their local doctor.

Not All Doctors Are Equal

Roughly 50 percent of doctors finished in the bottom half of their Medical School class. Just because someone didn’t have top marks in Medical School doesn’t mean that they don’t have adequate knowledge to treat an ailment. Perhaps the most important knowledge that a doctor needs is to know when he doesn’t know.

It is still challenging for patients to know whether they are dealing with someone who will help them. When you meet a doctor, you tend to judge them based on their “bedside manner.” Most of us look for someone who exudes confidence and seems to know what they are doing.

Confidence does not equal competence, and there are many doctors (and people in other fields) who have high levels of confidence in themselves but are not really competent to take care of the situation at hand.

Here is where doing some research can help. First, your doctor has online reviews, and those reviews will indicate something about the level of care they provide for patients. Second, if what your healthcare provider tells you seems really odd, it is easy to do a little research on the condition that you are supposedly dealing with and see if the symptoms line up and if the treatment seems reasonable.

It is important to realize that humans are not like vehicles. What I mean by that is that there is no scan tool that healthcare providers can hook up and generate all of the error codes and then fix the things that generate those codes.

Even if healthcare providers are certain of the diagnosis, some patients do not respond to the first or even the second treatment that is available. That doesn’t mean that the diagnosis or the treatment was wrong, but that people are not clones of each other and some respond better to one type of treatment than another.

Maybe someday we will have some type of genetic testing that tells us right off what the perfect medication or treatment plan is for a given illness, but that day seems a long way off.

A final thing to mention is that good doctors will not feel threatened by their patients asking questions or doing research. There are times when a patient will ask me about a new treatment that I am not familiar with, and I need to do my own research.

Those scenarios are not upsetting for me but rather a learning opportunity. “I’m not familiar with that,” I will tell my patient. “Let me do a little research and talk to some specialists that I trust, and I will call you later this week and let you know what I find out.”

Sometimes I investigate and find that the treatment is expensive and seems to provide mixed or little benefit, but sometimes it is an improvement over the past ways of doing things. Doctors need to learn and adjust their style of practicing medicine as we learn new things about diseases and how the human body responds to them.

Humility is Needed

The longer I practice medicine, the less I feel that I know. It isn’t that I have developed dementia, but rather that I realize that there are numerous diseases that we don’t have good treatments for. The human body is amazingly complex. There are 36 trillion cells in the human body, and normally, they all work together perfectly; the problem is figuring out what to do when they don’t.

The Dunning-Kruger Effect is something that affects many fields in which people with limited knowledge and skill significantly overestimate their abilities in that field. Studies have shown that 65 percent of Americans believe that they have above-average IQs.4 Statistically, this isn’t possible. Fifty percent of any group of people will have above-average IQs, and the other 50 percent will be below-average. That’s how the IQ scale is set up.

While this effect is present for doctors, it is also present for patients. “Doing your research” is not the same thing as spending four years in Medical School, another three years in a residency training program, and continuing to stay abreast of developments in medicine through a variety of educational courses. We all would do well to listen better and realize our limitations.

The fact that your mother’s cousin took milkweed extract and felt much better from similar symptoms to yours is interesting. Whether the milkweed extract helped them get over their illness, whether there was a placebo effect, or they were just going to get better anyway, regardless of what they took, is up for debate.

True Wisdom

I have mentioned wisdom already, and I would finish with that. True wisdom is realizing that healing comes from God. Psalms 103:3 says of God, “Who forgiveth all thine iniquities; who healeth all thy diseases.”

Healing doesn’t come from antibiotics or chemotherapy. It doesn’t come from taking the right supplements or even eating a healthy diet. Healing comes because God touches us, right down to the tiniest parts of our cells and immune system, and makes things whole again.

I do believe that sometimes He works through medicine, but other times He works through the effective, fervent prayer of righteous men and women. (James 5:16)

With all of our knowledge, it is easy for us to get puffed up with pride and believe that we need no one else. We live in a world that is teeming with knowledge and a world in which wisdom has taken a back seat.

We must choose the source of our information carefully and realize that we don’t know everything. Maybe the reason why the fear of the Lord is the beginning of wisdom is because it is the first step to us laying aside our pride and realizing that we are a tiny part of Creation. Only then, can we humbly listen and learn and receive healing.

“Så, vad förde dig hit idag?” frågade jag Ben, en 40-årig man som satt mitt emot mig.

“Tja,” svarade han. “Jag har några olika symtom. Det största är att jag alltid är trött, men jag har också gått upp i vikt, och knäna gör lite ont på morgnarna.”

Jag började mentalt gå igenom vad läkare kallar en differentialdiagnos – saker som kan orsaka den samling symtom som en patient har. Jag låter vanligtvis patienten förklara vilka symtom han upplever och ställer sedan frågor för att försöka komma fram till den specifika diagnosen.

Ben fortsatte ett tag till. Sedan plockade han fram ett papper. “Så, doktor,” sa han till mig. “Jag har gjort lite research kring min diagnos, och jag tror att det här är tester som jag behöver få gjorda för att utreda det.”

Jag tittade på listan. Den var ganska lång och innehöll några saker jag förmodligen skulle ha beställt ändå, som ett blodvärde och sköldkörtelstatus, men också några mycket märkliga saker som en nivå av vitamin B1 och en DHEA-nivå. Han ville också ha en CT-skanning av huvud, bröstkorg och buk.

“Det här är mycket provtagning,” sa jag. “Jag är inte säker på att vi behöver göra allt detta. Kan vi prata lite mer om dina symtom och sedan försöka avgränsa vilka tester som vore bäst för att reda ut det?”

Ben var inte imponerad. “Jag har gjort min research!” sa han bestämt. “Nuförtiden, med internet, kan du ta reda på saker som din läkare inte skulle berätta för dig – kanske saker han inte ens vet att testa för. Problemet är att jag behöver DIG för att beställa de här sakerna åt mig så att min försäkring täcker dem. Annars hade jag inte ens varit här.”

Med det lämnar vi Ben och hans obekväma läkare bakom oss. Det har alltid funnits patienter som kommit in med artiklar från tidningar som berättar för läsaren, “Sex saker din läkare inte kommer att berätta för dig om din hälsa” och listar vilka tester som borde göras. Det verkar som om det har blivit värre.

Många patienter vet mer än sina läkare. De kan söka efter sina symtom på webben och hitta alla möjliga saker som kan orsaka dessa symtom.

Utöver det är artificiell intelligens smart. ChatGPT, en plattform för artificiell intelligens, kunde klara de tre delarna av den amerikanska läkarlicensieringsprovet (USMLE).1 Den klarade sig inte särskilt bra – den fick precis över godkänt, men jag antar att det är tillräckligt bra för att den skulle kunna öppna ett mottagande tvärs över gatan från mitt och börja ta emot patienter.

I vissa avseenden är det bra att patienterna får tillgång till sådan nivå av information. Läkare är inte någon form av överpräst som har särskilda rättigheter att få tillgång till det allra heligaste inom medicinsk information. Dessutom är läkare långt ifrån perfekta, och man behöver bara läsa recensioner online för att se att de inte lyssnar väl, misslyckas med procedurer och kämpar med svåra diagnoser.

Det kan dock vara utmanande när patienter tror att de vet mer än sin läkare. Jag har alltid sagt att om du vet mer än din läkare behöver du antingen en rejäl dos ödmjukhet eller en ny läkare – eller kanske både och.

Skaffa vishet!

Ordspråksboken 4:5-9 säger: “Få vishet, få förstånd; glöm det inte och vika icke ifrån mina ord. Hör icke ifrån det, så skall hon bevara dig; älska henne, så skall hon vaka över dig. Vishet är det främsta; därför skaffa vishet; och med allt vad du äger, skaffa förstånd. Upphäv henne, så skall hon upphöja dig; hon skall framföra dig till ära, när du omfamnar henne. Hon skall sätta ett härligt prydnad på ditt huvud, en krona av ära skall hon skänka dig.”

Ordspråksboken 18:15 talar om att skaffa kunskap, men den antyder att innan vi söker kunskap bör vi försäkra oss om att vi har vishet och förstånd.

Författaren till Ordspråksboken var Salomo. Vi vet att tidigt i hans regeringstid hade han en dröm där Gud uppenbarade sig för honom och erbjöd vad han önskade. I sin ödmjukhet bad Salomo om ett förståndshjärta, så att han klokt skulle kunna leda ett så stort folk (1 Kungaboken 3:9,10).

När vi ser på kunskap är det helt enkelt en samling fakta – informationsblock som behöver sättas ihop till något slags sammanhängande mönster. Vishet och förstånd är verktygen med vilka vi ger mening åt den kunskap vi har förvärvat.

Vishet låter oss också bedöma hur tillförlitliga källorna till “kunskap” är. Den hjälper oss att ställa frågan: “Försöker den här personen sälja mig något? Har de verkligen några vetenskapliga studier som visar att det de säger är sant?”

Detta är två frågor jag ställer när jag tittar på en webbplats. Finns det länkar till produkter som säljs till mig, och är reklamen tydligt åtskild från artiklarna? Dessutom, finns det länkar till studier som stöder det som påstås? Om det finns, hur stora var dessa studier? Om en studie bara har 12 personer i sig är den inte tillräckligt stor för att ge pålitlig information.

Robert Harris gjorde akronymen CARS som hjälper till att avgöra om information på en webbplats är giltig. Credibility (trovärdighet), Accuracy (tidigare riktighet), Reasonableness (skälighet) och Supporting information (stödjande information) är alla viktiga att titta på för att se om vi bör värdera informationen på en webbplats.2

Tyvärr försöker många som påstår sig ha svaren för att leva länge och hälsosamt i själva verket sälja böcker, kosttillskott och en mängd andra produkter. En framträdande läkare som främjar bättre hälsa genom kosttillskott (som han själv säljer) har genom processen lyckats samla tillräckligt med pengar för att i en förklaring 2017 uppge att han var värd över 100 miljoner dollar. Det betyder inte att han inte har något att erbjuda, men det säger att han har en viss partiskhet i riktning mot att rekommendera saker han säljer.

American Medical Association har riktlinjer för att läkare etiskt ska kunna sälja produkter från sina mottagningar. De riktlinjerna säger att produkterna bör fylla ett särskilt akut behov (till exempel kryckor på en ortopedmottagning), ha vetenskaplig grund för sin användning, och att läkare bör erbjuda information om andra sätt patienterna kan få samma produkter någon annanstans.3 Dessutom bör läkare avslöja för sina patienter om de har något ekonomiskt intresse i produkten som erbjuds patienten.

Bekräftelsebias

De flesta av oss läser för att bekräfta det vi redan tror. Jag ser detta när människor läser Bibeln – på något sätt kan människor läsa Bibeln och helt ignorera skrifter som motsäger deras beteenden i fråga om politiskt engagemang eller blygsam klädsel men ändå tro att de följer allt i Skriften.

På samma sätt kan var och en av oss hitta berättelser och information som förstärker våra uppfattningar om läkare och medicin. Om vi tror att läkare bara är ute efter pengar och är oetiska och ordinerar läkemedel som är giftiga för patienter, kan vi hitta artiklar som bekräftar det. Å andra sidan, om vi söker efter berättelser som nedmonterar alternativmedicinska teorier, kan vi också hitta sådana artiklar.

Det viktiga är att vi närmar oss frågan för att söka verkliga svar och inser att vetenskapen inte vet allt.

Som exempel har vi inte bra behandlingar för människor som har långvariga COVID-symtom (Long COVID). Det betyder inte att många som led genom COVID inte månader senare lider av saker som mental dimma och trötthet, men det betyder att det inte finns något enskilt läkemedel som i studier har visat sig vara bättre än sockerpiller för att bli av med dessa symtom.

I avsaknad av vetenskapligt bevisade behandlingsplaner har många kliniker utvecklat egna behandlingsförlopp, med en blandning av kosttillskott och till och med hyperbar syrgasbehandlingar. Är dessa hjälpsamma? Det vet jag inte, men jag vet att de som marknadsför dem självsäkert kommer att hävda att de har en mycket hög framgångsgrad i att bota människor om de bara är villiga att följa (och betala för) behandlingsplanen.

Dessutom tenderar människor, när de forskar om sina symtom, att välja vilka diagnoser de tror är sannolika baserat på sina grundläggande personlighetstyper. Vissa människor är benägna att catastrophisera – det vill säga de tror omedelbart det värsta tänkbara utfallet av varje given situation de ställs inför. Dessa personer skriver in sina symtom och kommer fram till att de har cancer och bara har dagar eller veckor kvar att leva. Som Gud sade till Hiskia, är det tid för dem att ställa sitt hus i ordning.

Å andra sidan finns det många människor som är optimistiska av naturen. De skriver in sin symtomlista och kommer till slutsatsen att de har en mild virusinfektion och kommer att må bättre om några dagar.

Hela poängen med att ha en vårdgivare som går igenom saker är att praktikern kan (förhoppningsvis) sortera ut det troliga från det otroliga. De har inte den emotionella överlagringen som patienterna har, så de kan objektivt avgöra hur många tester som ska beställas och vilken typ av tester som bör göras för att komma fram till en diagnos.

Läkare kan identifiera farliga situationer

Jag minns att jag träffade en patient för många år sedan som kom in till mig med vad hon trodde var en bihåleinflammation. Hon var i 20-årsåldern och sa att hon hade en dunkande känsla i huvudet och mycket tryck.

Hon hade egentligen inte något näsflöde eller feber och inga av de typiska symtomen på bihåleinflammation, men bihåleinflammation verkade vara den mest sannolika diagnos hon kunde komma fram till.

Jag tittade på henne och gillade inte vad jag såg. För det första var hon extremt blek. För det andra var hennes puls ganska hög – 130 slag per minut i vila. När jag undersökte henne fann jag inget som tydde på att hon hade en bihåleinflammation.

“Jenny,” sa jag till henne. “Jag behöver att du åker till sjukhuset och tar ett akut blodstatusprov. Jag är rädd att du är mycket anemisk – även om jag inte vet varför. Vänta vid labbet så talar jag med dig när jag fått resultaten.”

Det var kanske 20 minuter senare som jag fick ett brådskande samtal från sjukhusets laboratorium. “Dr. Waldron,” sa rösten i andra änden. “Vi har ett kritiskt laboratoriesultat åt dig…”

Jennys hemoglobin var 4,6 (normalt är mellan 12 och 16), och hon fick slutligen en transfusion. Vad hon inte fick var behandling för en bihåleinflammation.

Bröstsmärta är ett klassiskt symtom som kan peka på ett underliggande hjärttillstånd. Samtidigt kan det helt enkelt indikera esofageal reflux (syra i matstrupen) eller inflammation i en revben eller muskel. Jag ser förmodligen ett par patienter varje dag som har detta symtom.

Majoriteten av dem behöver en enkel behandling, men några av dem måste skickas akut till sjukhuset för en fullständig hjärtutredning. Jag vet inte hur en sökmotor online ska veta i vilken riktning den ska peka för en person efter att ha granskat deras symtom.

I bästa fall kommer en onlinekälla att hänvisa en användare att söka akutsjukvård eller sin lokala läkare.

Alla läkare är inte lika

Cirka 50 procent av läkarna hamnade i den nedre halvan av sin läkarutbildningsklass. Bara för att någon inte hade topplaceringar i läkarutbildningen betyder det inte att de inte har tillräcklig kunskap för att behandla ett åkomma. Kanske är den viktigaste kunskapen en läkare behöver att veta när han inte vet.

Det är fortfarande utmanande för patienter att veta om de har att göra med någon som kommer att hjälpa dem. När du möter en läkare tenderar du att bedöma dem baserat på deras “sängkantsmanér”. De flesta av oss söker någon som utstrålar självförtroende och verkar veta vad de gör.

Självförtroende är inte liktydigt med kompetens, och det finns många läkare (och personer i andra yrkesfält) som har hög grad av självförtroende men inte verkligen är kompetenta att ta hand om den aktuella situationen.

Här kan det hjälpa att göra lite research. För det första har din läkare recensioner online, och dessa recensioner kommer att säga något om nivån på den vård de ger patienter. För det andra, om det din vårdgivare berättar för dig verkar riktigt märkligt, är det lätt att göra lite efterforskning om det tillstånd du uppges ha och se om symtomen stämmer och om behandlingen verkar rimlig.

Det är viktigt att inse att människor inte är som fordon. Vad jag menar med det är att det inte finns något skanningsverktyg som vårdgivare kan koppla upp och generera alla felkoder och sedan fixa det som genererar dessa koder.

Även om vårdgivare är säkra på diagnosen, svarar vissa patienter inte på den första eller ens den andra behandlingen som finns. Det betyder inte att diagnosen eller behandlingen var fel, utan att människor inte är kloner av varandra och vissa svarar bättre på en typ av behandling än en annan.

Kanske en dag kommer vi att ha någon typ av genetisk testning som direkt talar om vilket den perfekta medicinen eller behandlingsplanen är för en given sjukdom, men den dagen verkar ligga långt borta.

Avslutningsvis bör goda läkare inte känna sig hotade av att deras patienter ställer frågor eller gör research. Det finns gånger när en patient frågar mig om en ny behandling som jag inte är bekant med, och jag behöver göra min egen research.

Dessa scenarier upprör mig inte utan är snarare en möjlighet att lära. “Det där känner jag inte till,” säger jag till min patient. “Låt mig göra lite research och prata med några specialister jag litar på, så ringer jag dig senare i veckan och berättar vad jag hittar.”

Ibland undersöker jag och finner att behandlingen är dyr och verkar ge blandade eller små fördelar, men ibland är den en förbättring jämfört med tidigare sätt att göra saker. Läkare behöver lära sig och anpassa sitt sätt att utöva medicin när vi lär oss nya saker om sjukdomar och hur människokroppen svarar på dem.

Ödmjukhet behövs

Ju längre jag praktiserar medicin, desto mindre känner jag att jag vet. Det är inte så att jag har utvecklat demens, utan snarare att jag inser att det finns otaliga sjukdomar som vi inte har bra behandlingar för. Människokroppen är förbluffande komplex. Det finns 36 biljoner celler i människokroppen, och normalt samarbetar de alla perfekt; problemet är att lista ut vad man ska göra när de inte gör det.

Dunning–Kruger-effekten är något som påverkar många fält där människor med begränsad kunskap och skicklighet kraftigt överskattar sina förmågor inom det området. Studier har visat att 65 procent av amerikanerna tror att de har över genomsnittlig intelligens.4 Statistiskt sett är detta inte möjligt. Femtioprocent av en grupp människor kommer att ha över genomsnittlig intelligens, och de andra 50 procenten kommer att vara under genomsnittet. Så är IQ-skalan uppsatt.

Medan denna effekt finns hos läkare, finns den också hos patienter. “Att göra din research” är inte samma sak som att tillbringa fyra år i läkarutbildning, ytterligare tre år i ett AT- eller ST-program och fortsätta hålla sig à jour med utvecklingen inom medicin genom en mängd utbildningskurser. Vi skulle alla göra väl i att lyssna bättre och inse våra begränsningar.

Det faktum att din mammas kusin tog utdrag av mjölkört och kände sig mycket bättre från liknande symtom som dina är intressant. Huruvida mjölkörtsextraktet hjälpte dem att bli friskare, om det fanns en placeboeffekt, eller om de helt enkelt skulle blivit bättre ändå oavsett vad de tog, är öppet för debatt.

Verklig vishet

Jag har redan nämnt vishet, och jag vill avsluta med det. Verklig vishet är att inse att helande kommer från Gud. Psaltaren 103:3 säger om Gud: “Han som förlåter alla dina misstag, som helar alla dina sjukdomar.”

Helande kommer inte från antibiotika eller kemoterapi. Det kommer inte från att ta rätt tillskott eller ens att äta en hälsosam diet. Helande kommer därför att Gud rör vid oss, ner i de minsta delarna av våra celler och immunsystem, och gör oss hela igen.

Jag tror att han ibland verkar genom medicin, men andra gånger verkar han genom den rättfärdiges böns verksamma, ivriga förbön. (Jakobsbrevet 5:16)

Med all vår kunskap är det lätt för oss att bli uppblåsta av stolthet och tro att vi inte behöver någon annan. Vi lever i en värld som vimlar av kunskap och i en värld där vishet har fått stå tillbaka.

Vi måste välja vår informationskälla noggrant och inse att vi inte vet allt. Kanske är anledningen till att fruktan för Herren är vishetens begynnelse därför att det är det första steget för att lägga åt sidan vår stolthet och inse att vi är en liten del av skapelsen. Först då kan vi ödmjukt lyssna, lära och ta emot helande.

Use this scoring rubric: meaning/context/theological distinctions 50 points; completeness and factual/scripture-reference fidelity 30 points; target-language clarity/grammar/idiom 15 points; captions/alt/title/subtitle fidelity 5 points. A score is a review judgment, NOT a measured percentage of accuracy. Accept only a total of at least 95 and no major or critical finding.

A changed doctrinal assertion, negation, attribution, Scripture number, omitted substantive sentence, invented explanation, or untranslated substantive passage is major or critical and must prevent acceptance even when the numerical score is high. Preserve the author's theology rather than correcting it. Do not substitute another Bible version or require the translator to copy, retain, or restore English quoted prose as a fidelity workaround. Check paragraph meaning in context, headings, notes, captions, image descriptions, names, figures, and poetry. Do not penalize correct idiomatic expressions for failing to be literal. Do not flag mere stylistic alternatives as errors.
